tagline: A forest road along the southern fringe of the Adirondack High Peaks
intro: Blue Ridge Road winds through forest along the southern fringe of the Adirondack High Peaks, connecting Newcomb and North Hudson. New York’s transportation department identifies its scenic, natural and recreational qualities, with trails leading toward the Dix Mountain and Hoffman Notch wildernesses. The county-maintained portion is a two-lane rural highway, climbing beside Pine Hill and winding past mountain bases, brooks and ponds.

Named for Blue Ridge Falls, the road became part of NY 73 in the state’s 1930 highway renumbering. Around 1936, NY 73 was shortened and this stretch left the state highway system. The county road later carried the CR 2B designation; the short eastern section between the Northway and US 9 subsequently returned to state maintenance as NY 910K.

Driving east from NY 28N, the road initially follows the Hudson before meeting Tahawus Road, the side route north to the former mining village. The road crosses Vanderwhacker Brook and passes north of Cheney Pond before reaching the Boreas River hamlet. Beyond the Boreas River hamlet, it passes Sand Pond, descends beside Sand Pond Brook and runs along the base of Ragged Mountain. Farther east comes Palmer Pond, then the Northway interchange and the final stretch to US 9 in North Hudson.

moments.title: Tahawus
moments.text: The impurity that hindered ironmaking at Tahawus later became the reason to mine there again. Titanium dioxide made the iron ore difficult for nineteenth-century equipment to process. The Upper Works closed in 1857; a flood and a national economic crisis also contributed. In 1940, National Lead Industries reopened mining at the Lower Works to obtain titanium dioxide. A new community named Tahawus was established for the mine workers in 1943. At the old village, remnants of the 1854 McIntyre Blast Furnace survive, but most remaining building ruins belong to the later Tahawus Club era.

moments.title: Ragged Mountain
moments.text: At the base of Ragged Mountain, Blue Ridge Road follows the edge of the valley of a stream called The Branch. The approach from the west passes Sand Pond and descends beside Sand Pond Brook. Farther along, the road curves northeast at Three Brothers Mountain, then turns southeast into the hamlet of Blue Ridge.

moments.title: North Hudson
moments.text: Hemlock bark helped shape North Hudson’s early industry: the forests supplied tanning operations before trees were harvested for wood pulp. The town itself was formed from part of Moriah in 1848. By the end of the nineteenth century, tourism predominated, particularly at Underwood and Elk Lake. Frontier Town added a different kind of attraction in 1952, bringing a Wild West theme park to this Adirondack town. It operated until 1998; in 2018, Frontier Town reopened as a campground and day-use area. North Hudson’s hamlet sits by the Schroon River at the Northway and US 9.
